prompt: What happens when 2,4,6-trinitrochlorobenzene is treated with aqueous NaOH at room temperature?

choices.text: OH− substitutes for Cl−, giving 2,4,6-trinitrophenol
OH− removes a ring hydrogen, giving a benzyne
choices.why: The ring is activated by three nitro groups, so OH− simply adds and Cl− leaves. Benzyne forms from unactivated halobenzenes under harsh conditions.

choices.text: Nothing, because aryl halides don't react with nucleophiles
choices.why: Aryl halides with electron-withdrawing substituents do undergo nucleophilic substitution, and this one reacts even at room temperature.

choices.text: OH− replaces one of the nitro groups
choices.why: The leaving group is the chloride ion; the nitro groups stay and stabilize the intermediate.

explanation: Aryl halides that have electron-withdrawing substituents can undergo nucleophilic substitution. 2,4,6-Trinitrochlorobenzene reacts with aqueous NaOH at room temperature to give 2,4,6-trinitrophenol: the nucleophile OH− substitutes for Cl−.

prompt: What is Sanger's reagent, and what is it used for?

choices.text: 2,4-Dinitrofluorobenzene, used to label a protein's terminal NH2 group
2,4,6-Trinitrochlorobenzene, used to make 2,4,6-trinitrophenol
choices.why: That reaction is the section's first example of nucleophilic aromatic substitution, but Sanger's reagent is 2,4-dinitrofluorobenzene, used to label proteins.

choices.text: Fluorobenzene, used to label the side chains of all amino acids in a protein
choices.why: Sanger's reagent needs nitro groups to activate the ring, and it labels the terminal NH2 group at one end of the chain.

choices.text: 2,4-Dinitrofluorobenzene, used to remove the terminal amino acid by electrophilic substitution
choices.why: It labels the terminal NH2 group, and it reacts by nucleophilic aromatic substitution, with the amine as nucleophile.

explanation: One use of nucleophilic aromatic substitution is the reaction of proteins with 2,4-dinitrofluorobenzene, known as Sanger's reagent, which attaches a “label” to the terminal NH2 group of the amino acid at one end of the protein chain.

prompt: Why don't aryl halides react by an S_N1 mechanism?

choices.text: Losing the halide would form a very unstable aryl cation
The halo-substituted carbon is shielded from backside attack
choices.why: That's why aryl halides don't react by S_N2. S_N1 fails because the aryl cation is unstable.

choices.text: Aryl halides have no leaving group that can depart
choices.why: The halide is a leaving group; the problem is that losing it would give an unstable aryl cation.

choices.text: The aromatic ring is too electron-poor to lose a halide
choices.why: The section's reason is the instability of the aryl cation that would form.

explanation: S_N1 reactions don't occur with aryl halides because dissociation of the halide is energetically unfavorable, due to the instability of the potential aryl cation product.

prompt: Why don't aryl halides react by an S_N2 mechanism?

choices.text: The ring shields the carbon from backside approach, and inversion there is impossible
The aryl cation that would form along the way is too unstable
choices.why: That's why S_N1 fails. S_N2 has no cation; it fails because backside approach is blocked.

choices.text: The C–X bond of an aryl halide is too weak to take part
choices.why: The section's reason is geometric: the backside of the carbon is blocked by the ring.

choices.text: Aryl halides are too reactive and polymerize before substitution
choices.why: Aryl halides are inert to S_N2 conditions; the problem is that backside approach is impossible.

explanation: S_N2 reactions don't occur with aryl halides because the halo-substituted carbon of the aromatic ring is sterically shielded from a backside approach. A nucleophile would have to approach directly through the aromatic ring and invert the stereochemistry of the ring carbon, a geometric impossibility.

prompt: What intermediate forms in nucleophilic aromatic substitution?

choices.text: A negatively charged, resonance-stabilized Meisenheimer complex
A resonance-stabilized carbocation, formed when the halide leaves first
choices.why: The nucleophile adds first, before the halide leaves, so the intermediate is negatively charged.

choices.text: A benzyne, formed by elimination of HX
choices.why: Benzyne is the intermediate for unactivated aryl halides (Section 16.7). Activated aryl halides react through a Meisenheimer complex.

choices.text: A neutral aryl radical formed by loss of a halogen atom
choices.why: The mechanism is polar: the nucleophile adds to give a carbanion intermediate.

explanation: The nucleophile first adds to the electron-deficient aryl halide, forming a resonance-stabilized, negatively charged intermediate called a Meisenheimer complex. Halide ion is then eliminated (Figure 16.6.1).

prompt: Which chloronitrobenzene is inert to OH− at 130 °C?

choices.text: m-Chloronitrobenzene
o-Chloronitrobenzene
choices.why: With the nitro group ortho to the leaving group, the anion intermediate is stabilized by resonance, so the ortho isomer reacts.

choices.text: p-Chloronitrobenzene
choices.why: With the nitro group para to the leaving group, the anion intermediate is stabilized by resonance, so the para isomer reacts.

choices.text: All three are inert, because one nitro group isn't enough
choices.why: One nitro group is enough when it is ortho or para to the chlorine; those isomers react at 130 °C.

explanation: Nucleophilic aromatic substitution occurs only if an electron-withdrawing substituent is ortho or para to the leaving group, where it stabilizes the anion intermediate by resonance. A meta substituent offers no such stabilization, so o- and p-chloronitrobenzene react with OH− at 130 °C, but m-chloronitrobenzene is inert (Figure 16.6.2).

prompt: At what temperature, in °C, do p-chloronitrobenzene and o-chloronitrobenzene react with hydroxide ion to give substitution products?
explanation: p-Chloronitrobenzene and o-chloronitrobenzene react with hydroxide ion at 130 °C, but m-chloronitrobenzene is inert to OH−. Compare 2,4,6-trinitrochlorobenzene, with three activating nitro groups, which reacts at room temperature.

prompt: How do groups such as nitro, carbonyl, and cyano affect nucleophilic aromatic substitution, compared with electrophilic substitution?

choices.text: They activate the ring and direct ortho and para, the reverse of their electrophilic behavior
They deactivate the ring and direct meta in both kinds of substitution
choices.why: In nucleophilic substitution these groups stabilize the carbanion intermediate, so they activate the ring and work from ortho and para positions.

choices.text: They activate the ring and direct meta in both kinds of substitution
choices.why: In electrophilic substitution they deactivate; in nucleophilic substitution they act as ortho–para directors.

choices.text: They have no effect on nucleophilic substitution, which depends only on the halide
choices.why: Nucleophilic aromatic substitution needs such groups ortho or para to the leaving group to stabilize the anion intermediate.

explanation: Electrophilic substitutions are favored by electron-donating groups, which stabilize a carbocation intermediate, while nucleophilic substitutions are favored by electron-withdrawing groups, which stabilize a carbanion intermediate. So nitro, carbonyl, and cyano groups deactivate rings for electrophilic substitution but activate them for nucleophilic substitution; they are meta directors in the first and ortho–para directors in the second.

prompt: What does each kind of aromatic substitution replace on the ring?

choices.text: Electrophilic: a hydrogen; nucleophilic: a leaving group such as halide
Both replace a hydrogen on the ring
choices.why: Nucleophilic aromatic substitution replaces a leaving group, usually a halide ion.

choices.text: Electrophilic: a halide; nucleophilic: a hydrogen
choices.why: It's the other way around: electrophiles replace H+, and nucleophiles replace a leaving group such as Cl−.

choices.text: Both replace a halide ion on the ring
choices.why: Electrophilic substitutions replace hydrogen on the ring, as in the bromination of benzene.

explanation: Electrophilic substitutions replace hydrogen on the ring, while nucleophilic substitutions replace a leaving group, usually halide ion. For example, OH− replaces Cl− in 2,4,6-trinitrochlorobenzene, while Br+ replaces H+ in the bromination of benzene.

prompt: The herbicide oxyfluorfen is made from a phenol and an aryl fluoride (1-ethoxy-5-fluoro-2-nitrobenzene) using KOH. What happens?

choices.text: The phenoxide made by KOH displaces fluoride by nucleophilic aromatic substitution
The phenol is protonated, and the aryl fluoride attacks it in an electrophilic substitution
choices.why: KOH is a base: it removes the phenol's proton, making a nucleophilic phenoxide anion.

choices.text: The phenoxide anion displaces the fluoride by an S_N2 backside attack
choices.why: Aryl halides are inert to S_N2. The phenoxide adds to the ring, which is activated by the nitro group, and then fluoride leaves.

choices.text: KOH eliminates HF from the aryl fluoride to give a benzyne
choices.why: The ring carries an activating nitro group para to the fluorine, so the phenoxide adds directly in nucleophilic aromatic substitution.

explanation: Exercise 16.6.1: the phenol is deprotonated by KOH to give an anion that carries out a nucleophilic aromatic substitution on 1-ethoxy-5-fluoro-2-nitrobenzene. The nitro group, para to the fluorine, stabilizes the negatively charged intermediate.
